articles.title: Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal
articles.desc: For European carmakers, a hybrid quota offers some relief from lower-priced Chinese competition at a time when Volkswagen, Stellantis, Mercedes and BMW are under pressure on profits, though the cap’s generous starting size and annual increases limit how much market share it protects. Chinese brands
articles.content: For European carmakers, a hybrid quota offers some relief from lower-priced Chinese competition at a time when Volkswagen, Stellantis, Mercedes and BMW are under pressure on profits, though the cap’s generous starting size and annual increases limit how much market share it protects. Chinese brands that have leaned on hybrids to sidestep EU electric vehicle tariffs face slower European growth, with Chery among the most exposed. The bigger risk for markets is Thursday’s summit: a push by Germany and France for broader trade tools could invite retaliation, and Beijing’s control of rare earth supplies gives it leverage over the same European manufacturers the quota is meant to protect. --- Beijing has given Brussels a hybrid car quota and kept almost everything else, buying time before EU leaders decide how hard to push. Summary: The EU plans to limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to 350,000 a year, with the quota rising 6% annually from the second year and lasting four years The aim is for the safeguards to apply from December 1; they would technically cover hybrids from all countries to comply with WTO rules, with China’s quota at least as large as any other exporter’s The move follows a 16-point China-EU consensus on trade and investment reached in Beijing on Friday, with further talks planned for January and March Chinese brands took about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August, partly because hybrids escaped the EU’s 2024 tariffs on electric vehicles Analysts see the deal as a win for Beijing, which conceded little on the drivers of an EU trade deficit of more than €1 billion a day EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to consider a tougher response, with Germany and France pushing for stronger trade defence tools The European Union plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 a year, after Beijing agreed to curb exports as part of a 16-point trade and investment consensus reached in talks that ended on Friday. The proposed safeguards could take effect from December 1, Bloomberg News reported, citing a document outlining the measures. The quota would rise by 6% a year from the second year and remain in place for four years. To comply with World Trade Organization rules against discrimination, the limits would technically apply to hybrid imports from all countries, with China receiving a quota at least as large as any other exporter. Safeguards of this kind usually take the form of tariff-rate quotas, which leave imports below a set volume untouched and apply a levy to anything above it. The agreement followed talks in Beijing between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. Chinese hybrid shipments have surged partly because they escaped the tariffs Brussels imposed on fully electric vehicles in 2024, and Chinese brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August. EU ambassadors briefed on Sunday broadly welcomed the outcome but described it as only the start of efforts to rebalance trade. Analysts were less impressed. One China-focused research firm called the deal a strategic win for Beijing, arguing that beyond vehicles and modest tariff relief it does little to change China’s trading terms with Europe, while buying time for further talks in January and March. A trade law specialist said the timing suggested China wanted to ease tensions before EU leaders meet, and warned that WTO-compliant remedies often have limited impact on overall trade flows. The stakes for European industry are high. The EU’s trade deficit with China now exceeds €1 billion a day, and European carmakers are among the weakest performers globally. Mercedes-Benz car sales fell 8% in the third quarter, and Volkswagen cut its profit forecast last month. Renault Chief Executive Francois Provost welcomed the deal as a milestone, saying that without it Europe would face a damaging trade war. EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to decide whether to go further, after Germany and France called for stronger tools, including one that could restrict China’s access to the single market. Beijing has warned against protectionism, and its dominance of rare earth supplies gives it a powerful lever should Europe escalate. --- This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

The seized items include 35 types of narcotics such as hashish, cocaine, heroin, crystal meth, and Captagon pills, as well as 300 other prohibited materials. Customs ports also foiled
articles.content: RIYADH — Land, sea, and air customs ports across Saudi Arabia recorded 1,126 seizures of prohibited items last week. The seized items include 35 types of narcotics such as hashish, cocaine, heroin, crystal meth, and Captagon pills, as well as 300 other prohibited materials. Customs ports also foiled attempts to smuggle 810 tobacco products and their derivatives, in addition to eight types of cash. This was part of the ongoing efforts of the Zakat, Tax and Customs Authority (ZATCA) to strengthen security and protect society from all forms of prohibited substances.ZATCA reaffirmed its commitment to tightening customs control over the Kingdom’s imports and exports to safeguard society and ensure its security, through continuous cooperation and coordination with all relevant partner agencies. ZATCA urged the public to contribute to combating smuggling and protecting society and the national economy by reporting suspected violations through its dedicated security reporting number (1910), email (1910@zatca.gov.sa), or international number (009661910). The authority receives reports of smuggling crimes and violations of the provisions of the Unified Customs Law with complete confidentiality. Whistleblowers are also eligible for a financial reward if the information provided in their reports is verified as correct.

In its Goldman Sachs Corporate Day on Sep 30, Centurion Corporation highlighted H1FY26 revenue growth of 31 per cent to S$184.9 million and a 34 per cent increase in net profit from core business operations to S$87.7 million. The group said growth was driven by new bed capacity in Singapore, the consolidation of Westlite Mandai, contributions from EPIISOD Macquarie Park in Australia and the addition of the Harum Megah portfolio in Malaysia. The presentation also outlined a visible growth pipeline through 2028. As at Jun 30, the group managed approximately 85,528 beds and apartments across its worker accommodation, student accommodation, build-to-rent and key worker accommodation segments. Centurion expects portfolio capacity to increase to about 107,960 beds by 2028 through a combination of developments, acquisitions and asset enhancement initiatives across Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Hong Kong and the United Kingdom. articles.title: The Nobel Prize-winning science of optogenetics
articles.desc: The ability to switch on and off the brain's nerve cells with light has enabled research into many areas of medicine.
articles.content: The Nobel Prize-winning science of optogenetics | The Star The Nobel Prize-winning science of optogenetics Sunday, 11 Oct 2026 | 8:00 PM MYT Sabah must leverage science and technology to boost resource value, says deputy minister As the coding boom fades, computer science grads focus on AI skills in choppy job market Life sciences firm Danaher to launch AI-powered autonomous research lab in 2027 In optogenetics, scientists control neurons by stimulating them with light, potentially unlocking breakthroughs for conditions such as dementia, depression and blindness. Three scientists won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine last Monday (Oct 5, 2026) for their work in the field: American neurologist and Stanford University professor Dr Karl Deisseroth, 54; German biophysicist and Humboldt University of Berlin professor Dr Peter Hegemann, 71; and German biophysicist and University of Wuerzburg professor Dr Georg Nagel, 73. “Being able to manipulate cells with a combination of light and genetics has been transformational across the biological sciences,” said Imperial College London professor of neurotechnology Dr Simon Schultz. Here are some key facts about optogenetics and its uses. In a type of green algae, Prof Hegemann and Prof Nagel discovered a light-sensitive protein that they dubbed channelrhodopsin. Prof Deisseroth introduced it genetically into a cell and stimulated it with light, which triggered a nerve signal in rats and mice. Controlling the light, scientists can switch a neuron’s signal on and off with minute precision. By turning off some neurons and observing others, they can track which areas affect certain functions. Introducing the prize, Nobel medicine committee member and neuroscientist Prof Dr Abdel El Manira said the discovery shed light on functions “from parental behaviour and aggression to anxiety and fear, as well as fundamental physiological drives such as thirst and water intake”. Prof Schultz said his own teams had used optogenetics “as a closed loop treatment for memory disorders” by lengthening the pulses that help the brain store memories. “The next step is to demonstrate that we can improve learning and memory in complex tasks,” he said in comments released by Imperial College. United States’ University of Pittsburgh Medical School Department of Ophthalmology chairman Prof Dr Jose-Alain Sahel said that his team carried out promising trials using optogenetics to treat a degenerative disease. They used gene therapy to introduce the key protein to a patient’s defective eye cells and projected light through special goggles – successfully activating the retinal cells. “Vision restoration is probably the most fertile ground for relatively rapid medical advances” in the field, according to Cambridge University senior molecular biologist Dr Marco Tripodi in Britain. Beyond such direct therapeutic interventions, optogenetics could serve “as a discovery tool that reveals new therapeutic targets for neurological and psychiatric disease”, said Dr Tripodi. Epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease “provide obvious examples where the ability to control defined neuronal populations with high precision could ultimately be valuable”, he said. The prizewinning research could help “understand what goes wrong in diseases such as Alzheimer’s and epilepsy”, Spain’s CEU Cardenal Herrera University neural researcher Dr Jorge Brotons Mas said in comments published by Britain’s Science Media Centre. Research also aims to help address depression and anxiety disorders, several scientists said. Imperial College associate professor in bioengineering Dr Christopher Rowlands noted that there are “nascent trials” underway looking to use it to treat conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and addiction. Journalists at the award ceremony in Stockholm, Sweden, questioned the committee about whether the science shed light on parallels between real and artificial brains.
